svg.aria-label: Table of biblical places near Ramallah with their modern Arabic village names, scripture references and excavations
svg.text: the bible is a map of this district
Every one of these places is within a day’s walk of Ramallah, and every one of them is still called, in Arabic, what it was called three thousand years ago.
Ramallah’s own twin town. Robinson’s identification, and philologists doubt
it: al-Bīra most likely comes from Aramaic bīrāh, “fortress,” not the Hebrew
for “wells.” Six candidates have been proposed and none is secure. The town
is built over; nothing can be dug to settle it.
Where Samuel is said to have judged Israel and Saul to have been chosen
king; and where Gedaliah governed after 586. Badè, five seasons, 1926–35.
Abram pitches his tent between Bethel and Ai; Jacob dreams of the ladder and
names the place. Excavated by Albright and Kelso.
Hebrew ha-ʿAi means “the ruin” — and the
ground agrees. An Early Bronze town destroyed c. 2400 BC, then empty a
thousand years, then an Iron I village built on the mound without
Pritchard, 1956–59, found more than sixty jar
handles inscribed גבען — Gibeon, in eighth- and seventh-century
Hebrew script. The site says its own name.
The pass where Jonathan crossed between the two crags. The name came through
unbroken; the site is surveyed rather than excavated.
Absalom’s sheep-shearing. The highest summit of the central highlands, and
the horizon from Ramallah’s own rooftops.
Where the Gospel says Jesus withdrew with his disciples. Still today an
entirely Christian town, with a Byzantine church in it. Already an entry in
Hannah’s prayer, Eli, and the Ark before Jerusalem. Excavated by Danish and
Not one of these places was located by reading the Bible. They were located by asking the people who lived on them what they called home —
and the answers had been carried, in Arabic, by farming families on these hills for three thousand years. The Palestinian village names are why
the biblical map can be read at all. Where the ground has been dug it has agreed with them, and at al-Jib it agreed in writing.
